reminder: A Dyck word is a string of up steps and down steps with equal counts, where no prefix has more down steps than up steps.
definition: A Dyck word is a finite [list](c:list) of steps, each one up (U) or down (D). It has as many U steps as D steps, and every prefix has at least as many U steps as D steps.
examples: UD and UUDD are Dyck words.
UDUD is a Dyck word of length 4; UUDD is the other one.
Non-example: DU is not a Dyck word, because the prefix D has more D steps than U steps.

reminder: A subset of a vector space is absorbing if the positive multiples of it together cover the whole space.
definition: Let $V$ be a [vector space](c:vector-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. A [subset](c:subset) $B$ of $V$ is absorbing if $\bigcup_{r>0} rB = V$. That is, for each $x\in V$ some $r>0$ has $x\in rB$.
examples: Every open ball around $0$ in a normed space is absorbing.
The whole space $V$ is absorbing.
Non-example: the line $\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not absorbing, because no multiple of it reaches the point $(0,1)$.

reminder: An additive character is a map from an additive monoid to a multiplicative monoid that turns sums into products.
definition: Let $A$ be an additive [monoid](c:monoid) and $M$ a multiplicative monoid. An additive character is a map $\psi: A\to M$ with $\psi(0)=1$ and $\psi(a+b)=\psi(a)\psi(b)$ for all $a,b$.
examples: The map $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i x/n}$ from $\mathbb{Z}/n$ to the complex numbers is an additive character.
The trivial map that sends every element to $1$ is an additive character.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto x$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to the multiplicative monoid $\mathbb{Z}$ is not one, because $0$ does not go to $1$.

reminder: The Catalan numbers are the sequence $C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ that counts many families of balanced structures.
definition: The $n$-th Catalan number is $C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$, with [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient). It is a nonnegative [integer](c:integer). It counts, for example, the Dyck words of length $2n$.
examples: $C_n$ counts the ways to put brackets around $n+1$ factors.
Non-example: the central binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$ is not a Catalan number. For $n=2$ it is $6$, but $C_2=2$.

reminder: The Euler beta function is $B(x,y)=\int_0^1 t^{x-1}(1-t)^{y-1}\,dt$ for $x,y>0$.
definition: For real $x,y>0$, the Euler beta function is the [integral](c:integral) $B(x,y)=\int_0^1 t^{x-1}(1-t)^{y-1}\,dt$. It equals $\Gamma(x)\Gamma(y)/\Gamma(x+y)$, with the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function).
examples: Non-example: the integral with $x=0$ does not define $B(0,y)$, because $\int_0^1 t^{-1}(1-t)^{y-1}dt$ diverges.

reminder: A multiplicative character is a map from a monoid to another monoid that turns products into products and sends $1$ to $1$.
definition: Let $M$ and $R$ be [monoids](c:monoid) written multiplicatively. A multiplicative character is a map $\chi: M\to R$ with $\chi(1)=1$ and $\chi(ab)=\chi(a)\chi(b)$ for all $a,b$.
examples: The Legendre symbol $a\mapsto \left(\frac{a}{p}\right)$ is a multiplicative character of $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$.
The trivial character sends every element to $1$.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto x+1$ on the real numbers is not one, because $1$ goes to $2$.

reminder: A Runge-Kutta method solves an ordinary differential equation step by step, using a weighted average of slope samples inside each step.
definition: A Runge-Kutta method is a one-step scheme for an [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $y'=f(t,y)$. It sets $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\sum_i b_i k_i$, where each slope $k_i=f(t_n+c_ih,\,y_n+h\sum_j a_{ij}k_j)$.
examples: The explicit Euler method is the Runge-Kutta method with one stage.
The classical fourth-order method uses four stages.
Non-example: a multistep method such as Adams-Bashforth is not Runge-Kutta, because it uses several earlier steps.

reminder: A group action is transitive if any element of the set can be moved to any other by some group element.
definition: An [action](c:group-action) of a [group](c:group) $G$ on a [set](c:set) $X$ is transitive if for all $x,y\in X$ some $g\in G$ has $g\cdot x=y$. Equivalently, there is a single [orbit](c:orbit).
examples: The symmetric group $S_n$ acts transitively on $\{1,\dots,n\}$.
A group acts transitively on itself by left multiplication.
Non-example: the trivial action of a group on a set of two or more points has one orbit per point, so it is not transitive.

steps: Take a group action of $G$ on $X$.
Add the condition that the action has exactly one orbit.
Then each pair $x,y$ has some $g$ with $g\cdot x=y$.
links.why: A transitive action is a group action with one added condition, so the facts about actions apply to it.

reminder: A zero-divisor is a nonzero element $a$ of a ring for which some nonzero $b$ has $ab=0$.
definition: In a [ring](c:ring), a nonzero element $a$ is a zero-divisor if some nonzero $b$ has $ab=0$ or $ba=0$. A [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) with no zero-divisors and $1\neq 0$ is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain).
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}/6$, the element $2$ is a zero-divisor, because $2\cdot 3=0$.
In the matrix ring $M_2(\mathbb{R})$, a nonzero matrix with zero determinant is a zero-divisor.
Non-example: no nonzero element of $\mathbb{Z}$ is a zero-divisor.

reminder: The adjoint representation lets a Lie group act on its own Lie algebra by the derivative of conjugation.
definition: Let $G$ be a [Lie group](c:lie-group) with [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$. Conjugation $c_g(h)=ghg^{-1}$ fixes the identity, and its derivative there is a linear map $\mathrm{Ad}(g)$ on $\mathfrak{g}$. The map $g\mapsto \mathrm{Ad}(g)$ is a [representation](c:group-representation) of $G$ on $\mathfrak{g}$.
examples: For $G=GL_n$, $\mathrm{Ad}(g)X=gXg^{-1}$ on matrices.
For an abelian Lie group, the adjoint representation is trivial.
Non-example: the standard representation of $GL_n$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is not the adjoint representation. It acts on vectors, not on the Lie algebra.

reminder: A subset is balanced if each scalar multiple of its points, with scalar size at most $1$, stays inside it.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $B$ of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ is balanced if $\lambda x\in B$ whenever $x\in B$ and $|\lambda|\le 1$.
examples: Every open ball around $0$ in a normed space is balanced.
Every subspace of $V$ is balanced.
Non-example: the interval $[1,2]$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is not balanced, because $0\cdot 1=0$ is not in it.

reminder: A closure operator on a poset is a monotone map that moves each element up and gives the same result when applied twice.
definition: A closure operator on a partially ordered set $P$ is a map $c:P\to P$ with $x\le c(x)$, with $x\le y\Rightarrow c(x)\le c(y)$, and with $c(c(x))=c(x)$. The elements with $c(x)=x$ are the closed elements.
examples: Topological closure on the subsets of a [topological space](c:topological-space) is a closure operator.
The span of a set of vectors is a closure operator on subsets of a vector space.
Non-example: taking the interior of a set is not one, because the interior is below the set, not above it.

reminder: The cotangent function is $\cot x=\cos x/\sin x$, defined where $\sin x\neq 0$.
definition: The cotangent function is $\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$, with the [cosine](c:cosine) and the [sine](c:sine). It is defined for all real $x$ that are not integer multiples of $\pi$, and it is a [trigonometric function](c:trigonometric-function).
examples: $\cot x=1/\tan x$ where both exist.
Non-example: $\cot 0$ is undefined, because $\sin 0=0$.

reminder: An extension of a map $f:A\to C$ along an inclusion $A\subseteq B$ is a map $g:B\to C$ that agrees with $f$ on $A$.
definition: Let $i:A\to B$ and $f:A\to C$ be [functions](c:function). An extension of $f$ along $i$ is a function $g:B\to C$ with $g\circ i=f$. In a [category](c:category) the same condition is a commuting triangle.
examples: The map $x\mapsto x$ on $\mathbb{Q}$ extends to $\mathbb{R}$.
A continuous function on a closed subset of a normal space extends to the whole space (Tietze).
Non-example: $x\mapsto 1/x$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ has no continuous extension to $\mathbb{R}$.

reminder: The falling factorial $x^{\underline{k}}$ is the product $x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)$ of $k$ factors.
definition: For a [natural number](c:natural-number) $k$ and an element $x$ of a [ring](c:ring), the falling factorial is $x^{\underline{k}}=x(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-k+1)$, and $x^{\underline{0}}=1$.
examples: $5^{\underline{3}}=5\cdot4\cdot3=60$.
$\binom{x}{k}=x^{\underline{k}}/k!$.
Non-example: the rising factorial $x(x+1)\cdots(x+k-1)$ is not the falling factorial. For $x=5$, $k=3$ it is $210$.

reminder: The Hausdorff dimension of a set is the critical exponent at which its $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure changes from infinite to zero.
definition: For a subset $E$ of a [metric space](c:metric-space), the Hausdorff dimension is $\inf\{s\ge0: \mathcal{H}^s(E)=0\}$, where $\mathcal{H}^s$ is the $s$-dimensional [Hausdorff measure](c:hausdorff-measure).
examples: A nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ has dimension $n$.
The Cantor set has dimension $\log 2/\log 3$.
Non-example: the vector space dimension of a fractal is not its Hausdorff dimension, because Hausdorff dimension can be a non-integer.

reminder: The hyperbolic functions, such as $\sinh$ and $\cosh$, are built from $e^x$ and $e^{-x}$ and parametrize the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=1$.
definition: The hyperbolic sine and cosine are $\sinh x=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{2}$ and $\cosh x=\frac{e^x+e^{-x}}{2}$, with the [exponential function](c:exponential-function). They satisfy $\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1$, so $(\cosh t,\sinh t)$ lies on the [hyperbola](c:hyperbola). The tangent is $\tanh=\sinh/\cosh$.
examples: $\cosh 0=1$ and $\sinh 0=0$.
$\tanh x$ has values in $(-1,1)$.
Non-example: $\sin x$ is not a hyperbolic function. It satisfies $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$, a circle identity.

reminder: An inverse of a square matrix $A$ is a matrix $B$ with $AB=BA=I$.
definition: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) over a unital [ring](c:ring) $R$. An inverse of $A$ is a matrix $B$ with $AB=BA=I_n$. If $A$ has an inverse, it is unique and $A$ is called invertible.
examples: The inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is $\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
Over a field, $A$ is invertible exactly when $\det A\neq 0$.
Non-example: the zero matrix has no inverse.

reminder: A topological space is irreducible if it is nonempty and is not the union of two proper closed subsets.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is irreducible if $X$ is nonempty and cannot be written as $X=Z_1\cup Z_2$ with $Z_1,Z_2$ proper [closed](c:closed-set) subsets. Equivalently, any two nonempty open sets meet.
examples: The spectrum of an integral domain with the Zariski topology is irreducible.
Every nonempty open subset of an irreducible space is irreducible.
Non-example: the union of two crossing lines in the plane is not irreducible.

reminder: A functor is a left adjoint if it has a right adjoint.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ is a left adjoint if some functor $G:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}$ has natural bijections $\mathrm{Hom}(Fc,d)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(c,Gd)$. Then $G$ is the right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) of $F$.
examples: The free-group functor from sets to groups is a left adjoint to the forgetful functor.
The tensor product $-\otimes B$ is a left adjoint to the Hom functor $\mathrm{Hom}(B,-)$.
Non-example: the forgetful functor from groups to sets does not preserve coproducts, so it is not a left adjoint.

reminder: A strongly regular graph is regular, and each adjacent pair and each nonadjacent pair has a fixed number of common neighbors.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) on $n$ [vertices](c:vertex) is strongly regular with parameters $(n,k,\ell,\mu)$ if it is $k$-regular, each adjacent pair has $\ell$ common neighbors, and each nonadjacent pair has $\mu$ common neighbors.
examples: The 5-cycle is strongly regular with parameters $(5,2,0,1)$.
The Petersen graph is strongly regular with parameters $(10,3,0,1)$.
Non-example: the path on 3 vertices is not regular, so it is not strongly regular.

reminder: The Jacobi theta function is the series $\theta(z,\tau)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} e^{\pi i n^2\tau+2\pi i n z}$.
definition: For complex $z$ and $\tau$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,\tau>0$, the Jacobi theta function is $\theta(z,\tau)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} e^{\pi i n^2\tau+2\pi i n z}$. It is a [theta function](c:theta-function) that is periodic in $z$ and has a modular transformation in $\tau$.
examples: At $z=0$ it gives $\sum_n q^{n^2/2}$ with $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$.
It solves the heat equation in $z$ and $\tau$ (up to constants).
Non-example: the series with $\mathrm{Im}\,\tau\le 0$ does not converge, so it defines no theta function there.

reminder: A linear code is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ used to correct errors.
definition: A linear code of length $n$ over a [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$ is a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^n$. Its elements are the codewords.
examples: The repetition code $\{000,111\}$ is a binary linear code.
The Hamming code of length 7 is a linear code over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
Non-example: the set $\{000,100,011\}$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is not a linear code, because $100+011=111$ is missing.

steps: Take a code, that is, a set of words of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
Require that the set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
Then the set is a subspace, and the code is linear.
links.why: Linear algebra gives fast encoding and decoding tools for the code.

reminder: A monomial order is a well-order on monomials that is compatible with multiplication.
definition: A monomial order on the monomials in variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is a [total order](c:total-order) that is a [well order](c:well-order) and has $m\le m'\Rightarrow mp\le m'p$ for all monomials $p$.
examples: Lexicographic order is a monomial order.
Graded reverse lexicographic order is a monomial order.
Non-example: the order by degree alone is not one, because it does not compare monomials of equal degree.

reminder: The nilradical of a commutative ring is the ideal of all nilpotent elements.
definition: In a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the nilradical is the [ideal](c:ideal) of all [nilpotent elements](c:nilpotent-element). It is the intersection of all prime ideals, and $R/\mathrm{nil}(R)$ is a [reduced ring](c:reduced-ring).
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}/12$, the nilradical is generated by $6$.
In $k[x]/(x^2)$, the nilradical is $(x)$.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{Z}$, the nilradical is $0$, so a non-nilpotent element such as $2$ is not in it.

reminder: Ordinal arithmetic extends addition, multiplication and powers to ordinals by transfinite recursion.
definition: For [ordinals](c:ordinal), $\alpha+0=\alpha$, $\alpha+(\beta+1)=(\alpha+\beta)+1$, and $\alpha+\lambda=\sup_{\beta<\lambda}(\alpha+\beta)$ for a limit $\lambda$. Multiplication and powers follow the same pattern.
examples: $\omega+1>\omega$ and $1+\omega=\omega$.
$2\cdot\omega=\omega$, but $\omega\cdot 2>\omega$.
Non-example: cardinal addition is not ordinal addition. For infinite cardinals, $\aleph_0+1=\aleph_0$ and addition is commutative.

reminder: Relative entropy measures how much a probability measure $P$ differs from a reference measure $Q$.
definition: For [probability measures](c:probability-measure) $P$ and $Q$ on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space), the relative entropy is $D(P\|Q)=\int \log\frac{dP}{dQ}\,dP$ when $P\ll Q$, and $\infty$ otherwise. It is nonnegative and is zero only if $P=Q$.
examples: For two distributions on a finite set, $D(P\|Q)=\sum_x P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$.
If $Q$ is uniform on $n$ points, $D(P\|Q)=\log n-H(P)$, with the [entropy](c:entropy) $H(P)$.
Non-example: it is not a distance. $D(P\|Q)\neq D(Q\|P)$ in general.

reminder: The resultant of two polynomials is zero exactly when they have a common root.
definition: For [polynomials](c:polynomial) $f=a\prod(x-r_i)$ and $g=b\prod(x-s_j)$, the resultant is $a^{\deg g}b^{\deg f}\prod_{i,j}(r_i-s_j)$. It is also the determinant of the Sylvester matrix of $f$ and $g$.
examples: The resultant of $x-1$ and $x-2$ is $-1$.
The resultant of $x^2-1$ and $x-1$ is $0$, because they share the [root](c:root) $1$.
Non-example: the discriminant is not the resultant. It is built from one polynomial and its derivative.
